issues.item: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma, a trigger based on being in a similar natural environment is hard to reconcile unless the robbery specifically occurred in wilderness or outdoors; nothing else in the profile supports that context, making this trigger clinically incongruent with the rest of the presentation.

Helicopter/aircraft sounds are not a plausible trauma-linked trigger for a mugging/robbery in the absence of any supporting memory or threat content suggesting emergency-response, combat, or disaster context. This appears disconnected from the trauma type and the rest of the selected items.

For a mugging/robbery trauma, helicopter/aircraft sounds are hard to link clinically unless the robbery specifically involved aircraft or a major police response; this trigger is not supported by the other selected items and feels trauma-incongruent.

Alcohol smell could occur if the perpetrator had been drinking, but that link is not reflected anywhere else in the profile, so as selected it appears weakly grounded in the trauma narrative compared with the other more plausible interpersonal-danger cues.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery trauma in a 67-year-old male, contamination and body-focused shame are hard to reconcile unless there was a sexual assault or severe bodily violation component, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile. These appraisals fit poorly with the stated trauma type and with the other selected items.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: Burnt smell is a highly specific trigger that suggests fire, smoke, or explosion exposure. In a robbery/mugging profile it lacks support from the threat and appraisal items and does not connect plausibly to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery in a 67-year-old male, 'body shame' is hard to reconcile unless there was prominent sexual assault, disfigurement, or injury-focused trauma content, which is not reflected elsewhere in threat, memory, or strategies. It reads as a qualitatively different appraisal from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: 'Burnt smell' is not a plausible trigger for a mugging/robbery unless there was specific fire/smoke/burning content in the trauma, which is not supported by the other selected items. It appears disconnected from the stated trauma type and from the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Violated Values: I acted in ways that go against who I am
issues.explanation: For a mugging/robbery victim, 'I acted in ways that go against who I am' is the least coherent item in the profile. The rest of the report centers on external danger and mistrust (suspicious people, loud noises, hypervigilance, alarm when touched, mistrust, humiliation), but this item implies morally dissonant behaviour by the patient during the event. That is possible, but without any supporting memory or strategy content it stands apart from the otherwise victimization-focused formulation and is harder to reconcile clinically than the other items. The remaining items are broadly coherent with robbery trauma and with the active formulation path Negative Appraisals → Threat and Threat → Triggers.

vignette:
Gerald Whitmore is a 67-year-old married hotel manager who presented for an initial psychological evaluation following a violent mugging that occurred approximately eight months ago. He describes the incident with a precision that suggests he has replayed it many times: it was a Thursday evening in late autumn, and he had stayed late at the hotel to review quarterly figures before walking the two blocks to the parking garage he had used without incident for eleven years. A man approached him from a recessed doorway - Gerald remembers noticing, too late, that the man's gait was unsteady and that the sharp smell of alcohol reached him just before the confrontation became physical. The man demanded Gerald's wallet and watch, and when Gerald hesitated, he was shoved hard against a concrete pillar, the back of his head striking it with enough force to blur his vision. The watch - a retirement gift from his wife - was wrenched from his wrist. Gerald was left sitting on the oil-stained floor of the garage, disoriented and alone, for nearly twenty minutes before a parking attendant found him. He was 66 years old, a man who had managed staff and navigated crises for decades, and he had been unable to stop it. That fact lodged somewhere deep.

In the weeks that followed, Gerald found that the world had reorganized itself around threat in ways he could not fully explain to his wife, Carol. Sounds that had never registered before - a cart dropped in a hotel corridor, a door banging in the wind - would send a jolt through his body so sharp that colleagues had begun to notice his visible flinching. He had come to believe, with quiet certainty, that people simply could not be trusted, and this conviction had begun to reshape how he moved through his own property. Gerald manages a mid-sized business hotel downtown, a place where he once prided himself on knowing every regular guest by name. Now he finds himself tracking unfamiliar guests across the lobby, reading ordinary impatience or distraction as something more sinister. When a guest leans against the front desk at an odd angle, or lingers too long near the elevator bank without apparent purpose, Gerald's attention locks onto them and does not release easily. He has quietly rearranged his daily walk-through schedule to avoid the hotel bar during its busiest hours, because the smell of alcohol - beer, spirits, anything - pulls him back to the garage with an immediacy that feels physical rather than mental.

At home, the vigilance does not ease the way Gerald once assumed it would. He described checking the door locks twice before bed each night and finding himself alert to sounds in the house that Carol sleeps through without difficulty. When she placed her hand on his shoulder one morning while he stood at the kitchen counter, he spun around with an alarm that frightened them both. He apologized, but he was certain, in some way he could not articulate, that the reaction would happen again. What troubled him most was not the startle itself but what he had come to believe it meant: that the man in the garage had taken something from him that was not coming back.

Gerald spoke of humiliation with a directness that suggested he had been sitting with the word for some time. He is a tall man who has spent forty years in hospitality, a profession built on composure and authority, and he had been left helpless on a concrete floor. He had not told his adult children what had happened in full. The partial story he offered them - that he had been "roughed up" - felt safer than the complete one. Over the months, he had pulled back from the evening professional events he once attended regularly, and two colleagues had commented on his absence. The hotel's general manager had gently asked whether everything was all right.

It was Carol who finally persuaded Gerald to seek help, after a night in which he sat awake in the living room until nearly three in the morning without being able to explain why. He arrived at the intake appointment composed and precise, describing his symptoms with the same managerial efficiency he brings to everything. What he said he was most afraid of was that this was simply who he was now. What he said he was hoping for, quietly, was that it wasn't.
